findings.where: Article specimen: the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?' set against the article title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The subhead is about as large and as heavy as the article's title, and on phone it looks larger. Both are big, dark Gelasio in the same weight. Nothing in the type says which one is the page's title and which is a section inside it.
findings.who_objects: A reader of one of Mark's articles, who scrolls down and takes the subhead for the start of a new article. Angélique would also object: every subhead she adds will compete with the title, so long articles read as a stack of equal headlines.

findings.where: Motion sketch: its heading 'placed, calm, exact' (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: This is the only display heading on the page set in large Source Sans, and it is all lowercase. Every other heading uses Gelasio in sentence case: the hero line, the article title and the subhead. The page's own Type pair says Source Sans is only for 'the nav, the action, captions, dates and labels'. This heading breaks that rule and looks like a different site's tagline.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who is judging whether this tile's type system holds together. The page states a rule for its two faces and then breaks it in its own specimen. The lowercase sans slogan also leans towards the slick, startup tone the brief rules out.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'The World's Best…' and the Type pair caption ('Mark's voice…', 'Georgia's proportions')
findings.fault: These apostrophes are straight typewriter marks. Elsewhere the page uses curly marks: the subhead's ‘chapter topics’ and 'Mark’s own sentence' in the motion note. The mismatch is most visible in the article's largest line.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of a page that sells legal drafting and precision, who sees a typewriter apostrophe in a headline as careless. Angélique would also object, because the specimen does not show her which mark to use.

findings.where: First screen on phone: the lockup's subtitle 'Moseley Infrastructure Advisory Services' beside the mark
findings.fault: On phone the subtitle wraps and leaves 'Services' alone on its second line, under the name. The lockup looks ragged at the very top of the page.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the founder, because the name-and-logo lockup is the first thing a phone visitor sees. A broken line in it makes the identity look unfinished.
